explanations.explanation: God asks, "Does it not appear to you like nothing in comparison?" (Haggai 2:3) He asks it to the governor, the high priest and the remnant of the people. I think that question lands like a gut punch. But He isn't done talking, and what comes next is the good part.

I get the hope, friend. A bigger, shinier house would be nice. But God asks whether it appears "like nothing in comparison" (Haggai 2:3). The people are looking at it next to the former glory, and it doesn't measure up in their eyes.

Close, but no. God doesn't say it looks about the same. He asks, "Does it not appear to you like nothing in comparison?" (Haggai 2:3) That's a big gap, like comparing a full batch to one lonely crumb.

Three times, and I mean THREE, God says it: be strong. Be strong, Zerubbabel. Be strong, Joshua. Be strong, all you people of the land (Haggai 2:4). Nobody gets skipped. The governor, the high priest and everyday folks all get the same word.

Patience is a good thing, but it isn't what God says here. He tells Zerubbabel, Joshua and all the people of the land, "Be strong" (Haggai 2:4). Then He gives them the reason to stand tall: He is with them. Strong first, and then He tells them what to do.

I'll be honest, careful is what I'd say. I'd tell you to mind the oven and watch your mustache. But God says, "Be strong," to Zerubbabel, to Joshua and to all the people of the land (Haggai 2:4). He's lifting them up, not slowing them down.

"Work!" That's one word, and God doesn't dress it up. He follows it with, "For I am with you, declares the LORD of Hosts." (Haggai 2:4) So the work doesn't happen alone. Roll up your sleeves, friend, and know He's right there.
Rest is lovely, and I've done a lot of it, mostly in a drawer. But here God says, "Work!" (Haggai 2:4) The people are building His house. And He gives them a reason to keep going: "I am with you."

Waiting is a skill I know well, believe me. But God's word here is "Work!" (Haggai 2:4) Then He says, "For I am with you, declares the LORD of Hosts." He's telling them to get moving, not to sit still.

explanations.answer: When they came out of Egypt
explanations.explanation: God says, "This is the promise I made to you when you came out of Egypt." (Haggai 2:5) So this isn't a new promise cooked up this morning. It's an old one that's been in the oven a long, long time. And right after it, He says, "And My Spirit remains among you; do not be afraid."

The Jordan crossing was a big moment, but it's not the one God names. He says, "This is the promise I made to you when you came out of Egypt." (Haggai 2:5) That's even further back. The promise is older than most of what these people remember.

David, Israel's famous king, is a big name, but God doesn't point to him here. He says the promise was made "when you came out of Egypt." (Haggai 2:5) That's the moment He picks. It's an old promise, friend.

True! God says, "And My Spirit remains among you; do not be afraid." (Haggai 2:5) Remains, as in still there, not packing a bag. The Spirit hasn't left the building, and He's telling them not to be afraid.
This one's true, friend. God says, "And My Spirit remains among you; do not be afraid." (Haggai 2:5) The Spirit is still there with them. That's why He can tell them not to be afraid.

God says, "I will shake all the nations" (Haggai 2:7). First the heavens, the earth, the sea and the dry land, and then ALL the nations. He's not leaving anybody off the list. That's a big shake, baker.

City walls aren't on His list. God says He will shake "the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land" (Haggai 2:6), and then, "I will shake all the nations" (Haggai 2:7). Walls would be small potatoes next to that.

No palace gates here, friend. God says, "I will shake all the nations" (Haggai 2:7). That comes right after the heavens, the earth, the sea and the dry land (Haggai 2:6). The list gets bigger, not smaller.

Careful, this one's a trick. God doesn't say armies. He says the nations "will come with all their treasures" (Haggai 2:7). Treasures, not armies. Big difference when somebody's showing up at your door.
Right, the text says no such thing. God says the nations "will come with all their treasures" (Haggai 2:7). Armies never come up. Treasures are what show up.

Glory! God says, "I will fill this house with glory" (Haggai 2:7). This is the same house they were looking at like it was nothing. He doesn't say it needs more workers or more priests. He says He will fill it with glory.
The workers are busy, and God did tell them to work (Haggai 2:4). But the promise here is different. He says, "I will fill this house with glory" (Haggai 2:7). That's what He's filling it with.

Priests matter, and Joshua the high priest was right there in the audience (Haggai 2:2). But God doesn't say He'll fill the house with priests. He says, "I will fill this house with glory" (Haggai 2:7). Glory is the word.

"The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine, declares the LORD of Hosts." (Haggai 2:8) Plain and simple. The nations are bringing treasures, and God says the silver and gold belong to Him. I'd say that makes the delivery easy to sign for.
No king gets credit here. God says, "The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine, declares the LORD of Hosts." (Haggai 2:8) He's the One claiming it. No other owner is named.
Not the priests', friend. God says, "The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine, declares the LORD of Hosts." (Haggai 2:8) He claims it Himself. No other owner is named.

Flip it around, baker. God says, "The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former" (Haggai 2:9). Greater, not smaller. After all that talk of looking like nothing, that's quite a turnaround.

False is right, and I like how you caught it. God says, "The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former, says the LORD of Hosts." (Haggai 2:9) Greater, not smaller. The house that looked like nothing gets a big promise.
